newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Western envoys say Serb hardliners outside law.
newsitem.headline: Western envoys say Serb hardliners outside law.

text.p: Western envoys condemned Bosnian Serb hardliners on Monday for resorting to "totalitarian" propaganda in their power struggle with President Biljana Plavsic.
The international High Representative to Bosnia, Carlos Westendorp, described a vituperative attack on Plavsic in Bosnian Serb media as an attempt to sow fear and instability.

"It's clearly a deliberate attempt to destabilise the situation in Republika Srpska (the Serb Republic) and as such we wholeheartedly condemn it," Simon Haselock, spokesman for the High Representative, told reporters.

Haselock defended Plavsic's decision last week to dissolve the Bosnian Serb parliament as constitutional and said the major powers would not recognise attempts by government opponents to rewrite laws at "illegal" assembly sessions.

NATO commander General George Joulwan told reporters that international peacekeeping Stabilisation Force (SFOR) in Bosnia would not allow the power struggle to threaten the Dayton peace agreement or legal norms.

"We will support Dayton and we will support the democratic process. I would urge that there be no miscalulation by any of the parties on SFOR's intent to carry out its mandate," he said during a visit to Sarajevo.
Ultra-nationalists loyal to ex-president and indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic portrayed Plavsic on Sunday as a traitor bringing Bosnia's Serb entity to the "brink of ruin".

The Bosnian Serb news agency, under the strict control of Karadzic loyalists, said it had obtained a letter written by the army commander Pero Colic demanding Plavsic consult the military "before taking any further decision in this situation".
Diplomats expressed serious doubts about the authenticity of the letter as Bosnian Serb army generals had vowed to stay out of the confrontation last week.
They said the report, combined with moves to strip Plavsic of defence powers and rewrite laws to enable her recall, appeared to prepare the ground for a possible coup.
Plavsic said the letter showed the military had failed to stick to its promise not to take sides in the political conflict, which she called "the greatest sin of all".
United Nations officials confirmed that some police units in the northern town of Banja Luka had sided with Plavsic.

After dissolving the parliament last week, Plavsic was expected to form a new government soon and mediators were concerned two parallel authorities would compete for power, one in Banja Luka and the other directed by Karadzic in Pale, outside Sarajevo.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) mission, which is organising local elections set for September 13-14, said it was studying how to supervise general elections called by Plavsic for September 1. Karadzic loyalists have ignored her decision.
The conflict between Plavsic and Karadzic's circle erupted a week ago when the president tried to suspend the powerful interior minister, whom she accused of running smuggling rackets for Karadzic.

Although Plavsic is a nationalist ideologue, Western governments say she has shown a willingness, unlike Karadzic and his associates, to cooperate with the Dayton peace accords to obtain reconstruction aid and investment for Serb territory.
Karadzic was forced to step down a year ago due to his status as a suspect indicted by the U.N. war crimes tribunal.
Diplomats said Karadzic's blatant intervention to defend his inner circle had focused attention again on the threat posed by indicted war criminals to the peace process.

Fuelling speculation that Western policy might be shifting, U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen and a senior NATO official refused to rule out using allied troops to capture indicted war criminals in Bosnia, including Karadzic.

"Nothing has been ruled in or ruled out," Cohen told reporters on a plane bound for Madrid. "There has been no decision made. It has been the position of the (U.S.) administration that we will do whatever we can to strengthen the War Crimes Tribunal."
